_note: Standing lessons distilled from the owner's reviews (seeded 27 Oct 2026 from all notes so far). The writer, stager and judge read them every episode.

lessons.text: Never clip or trim the start of any spoken word; the first word of the video must be fully audible. Lengthen the video instead of cutting dialogue.
Every line is a complete, grammatical, natural Hindi/Hinglish sentence (e.g. 'almari mein hai', not 'almari mein'); no fragments or stock phrases like 'kitne sweet' or 'kyun takleef'.
Every line must make immediate sense to a first-time viewer; cut any line whose meaning needs explaining.
If a character is physically present in the scene, show them on screen; create and save a new character when the story needs one.
Any object the dialogue is about (box, gift, phone) must be visible in the right hands, or the staging must make it clearly off-screen; never show the wrong prop.
The ending must flow seamlessly into the opening (same framing, last line leads into the first, no audio jump).
Voice-only characters (phone, next room, doorway) must be as loud and clear as on-screen speakers.
When the owner asks for fixes, fix the same story with the smallest change; never write a new story unless the episode is dropped.
Relationships must be clear to a first-time viewer within the first seconds through natural cues (how people address each other, the place), never through exposition.
Back-and-forth must feel like real people talking: interruptions, reactions, uneven turns; no tidy line-for-line ping-pong.
Trying to be funny is not enough: every episode needs at least one real laugh-out-loud turn and a story the owner would enjoy; relatable theme alone fails.
Use festivals, events and trends in India and the world when timely, mixed with evergreen everyday stories; choose per episode.
Never force recurring characters or places (e.g. Rocky, the barber shop) into a story where they have no reason to be.
Expressions must be authentic and readable (one idea per face, symmetric eyes), lip sync must match the words, and heads must never distort.
